stories.headline: Why the Raiders named Fernando Mendoza as the starter
stories.summary: The Raiders named Fernando Mendoza as the starter shortly after trading Kirk Cousins to the Vikings.
stories.body:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- There isn't a particular moment that convinced the Las Vegas Raiders players and coaches that No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza was ready to be the team's starting quarterback. It's a collection of things the rookie has done since he arrived at the facility in April.

For coach Klint Kubiak, it's Mendoza's improvement in his accuracy and knowledge of the offense each week. A month ago, backup quarterback Aidan O'Connell recalled watching Mendoza make a few throws in practice, causing him to turn to quarterbacks coach Mike Sullivan and assistant head coach Mike McCoy and say, "Those were incredible."

Wide receiver Tre Tucker, on the other hand, knew Mendoza was capable of being QB1 when he watched the College Football Playoff National Championship game this past January and saw him lower his shoulder to knock off a Miami defender before diving into the end zone for a touchdown that helped Indiana secure its first-ever title.

"That shows you the kind of guy we are getting," Tucker said.

On Tuesday, Mendoza was named the starting quarterback after the Raiders traded veteran Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings. The Raiders' decision to move on from Cousins sent shock waves through the locker room. But with Mendoza, the first quarterback taken by the Raiders in the first round since 2007, waiting in the wings, the team knew this moment would come at some point.

As abrupt as the change of power might have felt, the Raiders believe Mendoza is ready for his starting debut Sunday against the Seattle Seahawks, the reigning Super Bowl champs and one of the league's most menacing defenses.

"Obviously there's a learning curve there, but Fernando is someone who just works extremely hard," starting center Tyler Linderbaum said. "... Anytime you get that with someone who wants to be great, and then on top of that has great mentors with them, I think it's very important. He's ready. We're ready."

The Raiders might have been more hesitant to move on from Cousins, who is second in the league in touchdown passes this season, if they felt Mendoza couldn't handle the role. To that point, Kubiak doesn't plan to make things easy for Mendoza in his debut.

Kubiak won't hold anything back from Mendoza and believes the 23-year-old signal-caller can operate the entire playbook. That confidence comes from Mendoza preparing as if he was the starter since Week 1.

"One of our mottos in the quarterback room is to always stay ready and always stay prepared," Mendoza said. "All three of us prepared like the starter. We were all in there doing our routine, doing it together, watching film together, going over the game plan together, tweaking and seeing which adjustments we'd like to make."

Mendoza went above and beyond to make sure he was ready in case his number was called. During games, Mendoza stood hip-to-hip with Sullivan. He wore his helmet while relaying the calls to Sullivan as delivered through the helmet communication device.

Sullivan said Mendoza became more comfortable rattling off plays and helped make in-game adjustments on the sideline with Cousins and O'Connell. At practice, when the first-team offense was getting reps, Mendoza was off to the side with Sullivan working on his footwork, pocket management and timing.

Playing with the scout team in practice, Mendoza impressed the coaching staff with the tight-window throws he made against the starting defense.

Sullivan said Mendoza also did a lot of extra work on his own. At night, Sullivan said Mendoza would be on the indoor practice field at the team's training facility with the game script on his phone. Mendoza would visualize the play and call it as he would in the huddle.

"He literally walks through the play and goes through what his reads [are], his pre-snap communication [and] footwork," Sullivan said. "His command of the offense, his ability to articulate the huddle calls [and] communicate at the line of scrimmage, has improved consistently. It's certainly credit to him."

Sullivan saw Mendoza's training come together in his NFL debut in Week 5's loss to the New England Patriots. The game was out of reach, but New England didn't take it easy on Mendoza.

The Patriots pressured Mendoza on 55.6% of his dropbacks, and he didn't flinch. He looked calmer and felt more in control of the offense compared with the preseason. Mendoza completed 6 of 8 passes for 48 yards during the Raiders' final possession.

"It's kind of hard to come off the bench at the end to get a feel for the game, and how they're rushing and how your offense is blocking, and he handled it like a champ," tight end Ian Thomas told ESPN. "I don't think anything different this upcoming week. He'll do the same thing."

Mendoza is not walking into a perfect situation. Sure, Brock Bowers has been one of the league's best tight ends. But the Raiders have lacked consistent production from their wide receivers outside of Tucker. The speedy wideout has 33 catches for 529 yards, while the rest of the receivers have 33 combined catches for 347 yards. Las Vegas has struggled to run the ball. On top of that, the defense has allowed opponents to score with ease over the past six weeks.

Mendoza, on the other hand, has been comfortable playing in difficult situations, dating back to his time at Christopher Columbus High School in Miami. During his senior season in 2021, Mendoza had to lead a young team that featured four new starters on the offensive line.

His former coach Dave Dunn said that was Mendoza's best season from a leadership standpoint because the team struggled in pass protection and didn't have the offensive weapons that it did in previous years. Dunn said Mendoza never complained and rallied the team to make a trip to the state semifinals.

"He was taking the brunt of the pass rush, and there were times when we couldn't throw it as we did in the past, but you could never tell in his demeanor that he was upset," Dunn told ESPN. "All he did was lead the team."

As a rookie, Mendoza doesn't have the knowledge that Cousins possesses from 15 years in the NFL. Tucker told ESPN that Mendoza, however, "has a different element to his game" that can help the Raiders. That element is Mendoza's mobility.

Mendoza's speed is not his strong suit by any means. Nonetheless, he can use his legs when necessary to escape pressure and extend plays.

"He's young. He will probably get out and scramble or whatever it is," Tucker said. "We always say, any guy that hasn't had a bunch of snaps, they got some fresh legs, so they're going to be out there running fast."

Mendoza will also allow Kubiak to incorporate more designed rollouts into the game plan. When Kubiak was the offensive coordinator for the Seahawks last season, starting quarterback Sam Darnold had a designed rollout rate of 11%. On designed rollouts, Darnold completed 42 of 56 passes (75%) for 656 yards, eight touchdowns and an interception.

In Las Vegas, Kubiak used designed rollouts on only 0.05% of Cousins' dropbacks. The expectation is for that number to increase with Mendoza under center.

"[Mendoza] brings his own unique things, and yes, he's a young man with some juice in his legs, and he's got a lot of talent," Kubiak said. "But in this game on Sunday, it's going to be about way more than his physical talent. It's going to be about his leadership, his knowledge of the offense [and] his ability to read defense."

The Raiders believe in Mendoza. At the same time, the rest of the team will have to do its part to ensure Mendoza's transition into the starting role is smooth. The Raiders can do that by fixing the run game, which has seemed like a tall task all season. But if they can establish a consistent rushing attack in the final eight games, that should take some pressure off Mendoza.

Based on what Mendoza showed in the preseason and his short playing time against New England, he's going to target the wide receivers quite a bit. That means Las Vegas will need more from its wideouts, especially against Seattle.

Tight ends Bowers and Michael Mayer have been relied on heavily in the passing game. Seattle will try to limit both players as much as possible, taking away opportunities in the middle of the field. Second-year safety Nick Emmanwori will most likely spend a lot of time matching up against Mayer. Last week, Emmanwori matched up against Arizona's star tight end Trey McBride eight times and didn't allow a catch on one target.

Meanwhile, cornerback Devon Witherspoon could be asked to defend Bowers since the All-Pro pass catcher spends most of his time lining up on the outside. In 52 coverage snaps against tight ends, Witherspoon has allowed seven catches for 36 yards and a passer rating of 68.8 on 11 targets.

"Every week in the NFL is tough, and this is the best defense in the NFL," Kubiak said. "Again, he's got to do his job and not worry about a whole lot else. Everybody does their one-eleventh, and everyone around him elevates their play."

O'Connell has made a "big attempt" to ensure Mendoza doesn't make his starting debut bigger than it has to be. Understanding the nerves that come with making an NFL start, O'Connell has tried to take Mendoza's mind off football just a bit.

In the practices leading up to Sunday, O'Connell said he joked around with Mendoza, shoving him in between periods to ease the tension.

"He's super locked in on football, which is awesome," O'Connell said. "He's just trying to do his best. [I'm] looking forward to it."

stories.headline: South Africa need to start Mbokazi in next AFCON qualifier against Kenya
stories.summary: After three wins in the first three games, Pitso Mosimane suffered a setback in a 2-2 draw against Kenya, which laid bare the importance of MLS trio Lyle Foster, Puso Dithejane and Mbekezeli Mbokazi.
stories.body:
After three wins in the first three games of his second stint as Bafana Bafana head coach, Pitso Mosimane suffered a setback in a 2-2 draw against Kenya at Orlando Amstel Arena which laid bare the importance of MLS trio Lyle Foster, Puso Dithejane and Mbekezeli Mbokazi.

Foster and Dithejane played well off the bench, while unused substitute Mbokazi's claim for a starting berth was strengthened by a late mistake from Olwethu Makhanya which allowed Ryan Ogam to score and an Ime Okon display which was short of his best.

It was somewhat surprising that Mbokazi played no part in the draw, but in fairness, Makhanya and Okon played well over the last international break while he was out injured and MLS players often take time to acclimatise over international breaks due to jetlag.

Mosimane's predecessor, Hugo Broos, had cited this as a potential reason for Bongokuhle Hlongwane's dip in form for South Africa after joining Minnesota United, and infamously criticised Mbokazi for joining Chicago Fire FC.

However, Mosimane is likely to turn to MLS stars to dig Bafana out of a tight position. For one, it was clear in Dithejane's late cameo after replacing Tshepang Moremi in the 57th minute that he is a better player than the one who joined the Fire from TS Galaxy in January.

The winger created several chances with his pinpoint crosses - and in fairness, Lyle Foster (on loan at Houston Dynamo from Burnley) should have put one away.

However, Foster provided the assist for a 77th-minute Relebohile Mofokeng stunner that appeared to have clinched the game until Ogam's late equaliser.

The hard truth is: Bafana Bafana does not have an in-form striker in national team colours. Rayners is playing well for Mamelodi Sundowns, but it has been some time since he replicated that form in front of goal for the national team.

Even when he is not in fine form in front of goal, Foster contributes to the team in other ways - as was evident in his role in the build-up to Mofokeng's stunner.

The Union Saint-Gilloise attacking midfielder is the one Bafana Bafana player who it is difficult to fault at all for Friday night's performance. He hit the post, scored a goal, and was creatively excellent throughout the game until he was substituted off in stoppage time for Cassius Mailula.

Bafana's MLS stars may not be in quite the same rich vein of form as Mofokeng at the moment, but their services are sorely needed.

South Africa will face Kenya again in Nairobi on Tuesday and at least one change is needed at centre-back, with Okon short of recent minutes for Hannover 96 and Makhanya in strong form for Rangers, but now coming off the back of a mistake.

Across the front four, not only Rayners - but also Tshepang Moremi - was not clinical enough on Friday. After scoring against Egypt in an October friendly and contributing off the bench against Kenya, Dithejane deserves a starting berth, while confidence player Foster deserves a chance to rediscover his shooting touch.

stories.headline: JuJu Watkins projected No. 1 WNBA pick in latest 2027 mock draft
stories.summary: JuJu Watkins, Madison Booker and Hannah Hidalgo are the projected top picks ahead of Sunday's WNBA draft lottery.
stories.body:
The college and pro women's basketball worlds align Sunday as two of the country's best teams face off, followed by the WNBA draft lottery.

No. 1 South Carolina and No. 3 USC meet in Greenville, South Carolina (ABC, 1 p.m. ET), a game that features multiple players in ESPN's second WNBA mock draft, led by the Trojans' JuJu Watkins.

She sat out last season because of a knee injury, so this is only her third college season. But age-wise, Watkins is eligible for the draft. Though we don't know yet if she will turn pro or return for another college season, for the mock draft purposes we continue to include her.

For that matter, there is also uncertainty about the seniors who have already completed three seasons. Under the NCAA's new age-based eligibility model -- the five-seasons-in-five-years rule -- they could return for the 2027-28 season. All of it means not only are the mock draft pick projections speculative, so is the draft pool.

For now, three Gamecocks also continue to be projected first-round picks, though Tessa Johnson, Chloe Kitts and Ashlyn Watkins moved up at least one spot.

We will find out the lottery results Sunday night (7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN) and who has the coveted No. 1 pick. For now, we have the Houston Comets (formerly the Connecticut Sun) and the Toronto Tempo at 1-2.

1. Houston Comets: JuJu Watkins
USC | guard | 6-foot-2 | senior

Watkins and the Trojans are already off to a fast start. The March 2025 knee injury that forced her to sit out last season doesn't seem to have slowed her down. Watkins is averaging 24.3 points, 8.3 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 3.7 steals heading into Sunday's matchup with South Carolina. Again, though we don't know for sure if she will declare for the draft, if she does, she is a franchise-changer.

2. Toronto Tempo: Madison Booker
Texas | forward | 6-foot-1 | senior

Like several teams, Texas has not been tested yet. But Booker has displayed why she's a lottery pick in the Longhorns' three victories so far, including a 30-point, six-assist game against Northern Colorado. Booker's size, strength and confidence on offense and her versatility on defense all should translate to the pro game.

3. Washington Mystics: Hannah Hidalgo
Notre Dame | guard | 5-foot-6 | senior

Hidalgo has carried a heavy load in her college career, and that continues in her senior season. In three blowout wins, she has averaged 27.3 points, 7.7 rebounds, 5.0 assists and 5.0 steals while shooting 58% from the field. Hidalgo is a huge threat on offense and defense, and could really add to a young core already there if she goes to the Mystics.

4. Seattle Storm: Kymora Johnson
Virginia | guard | 5-foot-7 | senior

The unranked Cavaliers are 4-0, and we will know more about them once they play their tougher nonconference foes, such as Oklahoma on Nov. 23. But so far, Johnson has looked very good, averaging 19.5 points, 4.0 rebounds, 4.5 assists and 2.5 steals while shooting 62.2% from the field and 61.1% from beyond the arc (11 of 18). Johnson has the most to prove among potential lottery picks, but she is off to a great start.

5. Portland Fire: Mikaylah Williams
LSU | guard | 6-foot | senior

The Tigers have cruised through three blowouts, so Williams' averages -- 18.7 points, 4.7 rebounds and 6.3 assists while shooting 58.8% from the field -- don't tell us anything we didn't expect. She's a very good, pro-ready player on the offensive end who will need to improve defensively in the WNBA -- and has the ability to do that.

6. Los Angeles Sparks: S'Mya Nichols
Kansas | guard | 6-foot | senior

Nichols is off to a slower start than expected, averaging 12.7 points and 3.7 assists (she averaged 17.4 and 4.6 last season). But to be fair, that has also been strategic for Nichols and the Jayhawks, who haven't needed that much from her in three comfortable wins. Look for her to be more her usual self as KU next faces ranked Nebraska and Minnesota.

7. Los Angeles Sparks: Sarah Cissé
France | forward | 6-foot-2

There's so much we don't know now about the Sparks -- including who their coach will be -- as they move on after Nneka Ogwumike's retirement. But Cissé could be another talented player out of France to make an impact on the WNBA. The MVP of the U20 European Championships this summer, she turns 20 in January.

8. New York Liberty: Tessa Johnson
South Carolina | guard | 6-foot-1 | senior

Johnson's 3-point shooting is an impressive tool that will translate to the pro game and could help her move up the draft board. She was the top power-conference player in the country last season in 3-point percentage (44.8%, 90 of 201). So far this season, she has made 6 of 14 (42.9%) from beyond the arc and is averaging 13.3 points.

9. Dallas Wings: Chloe Kitts
South Carolina | forward | 6-foot-2 | senior

Kitts sat out last season because of a knee injury but has looked very good so far. Like Johnson, she's another player who could move up the draft board. A starter as a junior in 2024-25, she averaged a career-best 10.2 points and 7.7 rebounds. Through three games this season, she has two double-doubles and is averaging 12.3 points and 9.7 rebounds.

10. Indiana Fever: Ashlyn Watkins
South Carolina | forward | 6-foot-3 | senior

Watkins' career numbers don't stand out. But she is a pro prospect because of her ability to defend multiple positions, her rebounding and her strength. Watkins was limited to 14 games by a knee injury in 2024-25, then didn't play last season as she recovered. This season, she hasn't gotten on track yet offensively, but is averaging 7.7 rebounds.

11. Chicago Sky: Ainhoa Risacher
France | forward | 6-foot-1

If you recognize the last name, Risacher is the younger sister of Zaccharie Risacher, the NBA's No. 1 draft pick in 2024. A good-sized wing player, Risacher competed alongside Cissé on France's winning U20 European Championships team this past summer. She will turn 20 in July.

12. Chicago Sky: MiLaysia Fulwiley
LSU | guard | 5-foot-11 | senior

Fulwiley is averaging 16.0 points, 4.0 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 4.7 steals for the Tigers, who have clobbered three overmatched opponents so far. Fulwiley, who can change games with her offense and defense, has a chance to move up the draft board if she shows more consistency now that she is a starter.

13. Dallas Wings: Talaysia Cooper
Ole Miss | guard | 6-foot-0 | senior

Cooper, playing for her third SEC program, is averaging 14.3 points and shooting 42.9% (9-of-21) from 3-point range. She showed progress from beyond the arc last season, and if that continues this season it will help her draft prospects. Cooper had her best defensive season as a sophomore at Tennessee, and a return to that level with Ole Miss will boost her.

14. Golden State Valkyries: Oluchi Okananwa
Maryland | guard | 5-foot-10 | senior

Okananwa is averaging 17.5 points and 7.5 rebounds, but the Terrapins have played only two games. She was first team all-Big Ten and all-defense last season -- we know the Valkyries love defense -- but she probably will need to show improvement as a 3-point shooter to ensure being a first-round pick.

15. Minnesota Lynx: Clara Strack
Kentucky | center | 6-foot-5 | senior

It's not easy for traditional centers to find their way in the WNBA, so having shooting range matters. Strack has shown that, making 42 3-pointers over the past two seasons, but she will need to keep improving. Strack, who was the SEC's defensive player of the year in 2025, is averaging 15.8 points, 7.5 rebounds and 3.8 blocks for the 4-0 Wildcats.

stories.headline: MMA stars Merab Dvalishvili, Usman Nurmagomedov brawl at hotel in Abu Dhabi
stories.summary: MMA stars Merab Dvalishvili and Usman Nurmagomedov got into a public brawl at a hotel in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.
stories.body:
Former UFC bantamweight champion Merab Dvalishvili and PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov were involved in a physical altercation Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, with video of the incident widely circulated on social media.

Dvalishvili, who is in Abu Dhabi ahead of Saturday's Real American Freestyle event, posted a video of his bloodied face after the scuffle. Multiple videos of the incident showed Nurmagomedov, whose older brother, Umar, lost a bantamweight title fight to Dvalishvili in 2025, approach Dvalishvili from behind and slap him in the face.

Former UFC lightweight champion Ilia Topuria, who is friends with Dvalishvili, shared video of the encounter online. Following the initial slap, Dvalishvili attempts to go after Nurmagomedov. A chaotic scene quickly unfolded, involving multiple members from the camps of both fighters. In his video afterward, Dvalishvili refers to Nurmagomedov and his camp as "snakes."

"What a sneaky way, guys," Dvalishvili says. "What kind of fighters you guys are? What kind of man does this? If you want to try, let's do it the real way."

Abu Dhabi Police issued a statement Thursday, saying eight people were arrested for their part in the brawl, though they did not name Dvalishvili and Nurmagomedov specifically. Additionally, two people who filmed the encounter were also taken arrested. It is not clear whether any or all of the detained parties remain in custody.

UFC president Dana White, speaking at a news conference Thursday, reacted to the altercation, calling it "absolutely ridiculous and stupid."

Wednesday's confrontation marks the latest in a long-running feud between Dvalishvili and the Nurmagomedov team. Before his win over Umar in January 2025, Dvalishvili referred to Umar as "spoiled" and accused the Dagestani of being disrespectful. The two camps were involved in a brief altercation in July at another RAF event in Georgia.

Both Merab and Umar are scheduled to compete at RAF on Saturday. Dvalishvili faces former UFC title challenger Marlon Moraes, while Nurmagomedov will wrestle former UFC champion Urijah Faber.

Usman Nurmagomedov is currently in a state of restricted free agency, with much speculation whether he will leave the PFL to fight in the UFC in 2027.

stories.headline: November Draft Power Rankings: ESPN's final, top 50 rankings ahead of the draft
stories.summary: It's time for ESPN's final AFL Draft Power Rankings for 2026. Jasper Chellappah has ranked his top 50 prospects for next week's draft, with all signs pointing to a deep and talented pool of prospects.
stories.body:
After eight iterations of ESPN's AFL Draft Power Rankings for 2026, the final top 50 is here.

A truly deep and talented pool of prospects has emerged across the season, with the final draft of the 18-team era filled to the brim with prospects deserving of AFL opportunities.

A total of around 65 talents will be selected, and amongst the 2008-born cohort are three mature-agers. Jake Soutar, Jack Slattery and Brady Wright should find homes in the AFL Draft as late-developing talents.

While it's a settled top 10 of the same names, there have been sliders and fallers across the top 50. Small forward George Dimer is receiving late first round interest and has the tools to excel at the next level despite his smaller frame, and Lachie Hicks has the athletic profile and work ethic to explode in a professional environment.

Debate has raged around Arki Butler's 2km time trial of 7:29, which would have been equal-slowest at the draft combine. The goalkicker remains a chance at Essendon's first, with his best 2km a minute faster completed in pre-season. Clubs won't be concerned about a power athlete's poor run first-up off a hamstring injury and he remains at No. 3 here as the best open pool prospect.

A deep crop means there are a host of unlucky names to not feature, though they remain good chances to be drafted across the night of November 19 and 20.

WA's Tom Brown provides reliability in defence and Kai Parker (Collingwood NGA) was cruelled by injury in his top-age campaign. Jordan Knapp is a proper ball magnet, Memphis Webb will have fans as a tough midfielder and Judd Burgiel boasts wheels streaming out of defence. Gus Kennedy, Jackson Watkins, Finlay Yeo, Harry Franz and Tate Hodgson are prominent names across the draft cycle that are unlucky not to feature.

A week out from the 2026 AFL Draft, this is ESPN's final top 50 Power Rankings.

Previous rankings: April | May | June | July | August | September | October | November

Other stuff to know: Draft primer and FAQs | Every club's needs | Draft order | Jasper's most recent Phantom Draft | Full combine wrap and results

1. Dougie Cochrane (Port Adelaide NGA) (previously: 1)

Central District/South Australia

FWD/MID/DEF, 195cm

For 24 months now Cochrane has been the pick 1 apparent in 2026. It's a testament to his talent that he's stuck at one despite never playing an U18 National Championships game and registering only four games this season. He has the size and aerial prowess to thrive as a key forward, the skills and athletic profile to dominate behind the ball and the ambition to move into the engine room and become a game-breaking midfielder. Cochrane is a truly unique prospect and a consensus top of the crop. Port Adelaide are the beneficiaries on draft night, but it remains to be seen what position the son of Stuey will play his best footy.

READ: Consensus top AFL draft prospect Dougie Cochrane already in rare air

2. Cody Walker (Carlton father-son) (2)

Bendigo Pioneers/Vic Country

MID, 184cm

National Championships: 3 games, 23.7 disposals, 3.7 clearances, 1.3 tackles

Walker blends natural talent with ambition and professionalism. He's an excellent stoppage player, winning his own ball and twisting out of trouble with sharp agility and a burst of acceleration. He finds exits few others can and has already looked a class above at VFL level through the midfield. Walker's decision-making and skill execution under pressure lets him down on occasion, but the son of former high-flying Blue Andrew is a top tier prospect with the upside of a future Brownlow Medallist.

READ: 'I'm a competitor': Cody Walker primed and ready for the next step

3. Arki Butler (3)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID/FWD, 182cm

National Championships: 3 games, 12.3 disposals, 7.0 marks, 1.7 goals

Few draft prospects have ever borne a resemblance to Butler. The powerfully-built medium forward boasts excellent hands in marking contests, craft with either foot at ground level, a violent fend off and elite burst to create separation. He's a matchwinner inside 50, exposing mismatches and stepping up when the game is on the line. Butler has had flashes of something special as a midfielder but could be too damaging up forward to ever become a permanent on-baller.

READ: 'All damage' - Arki Butler is the 2026 draft's most watchable junior footballer

4. Ethan Drever (4)

GWV Rebels/Vic Country

MID, 188cm

National Championships: 4 games, 20.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 4.2 tackles

Drever has all the tools to become a superstar midfielder. He can use his big frame to win contested ball, but is at his best in transition where his power and top speed changes the game. The Vic Country MVP thrives with the ball in space, making it his trademark to hit the paint of 50 and kick long-running goals all season. Drever is a high-floor prospect with leadership attributes at the next level.

READ: Power to burn and a 'trademark' goal: why Drever rocketed up draft boards

5. Harry Van Hattum (5)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

RUC/FWD, 205cm

National Championships: 4 games, 10.8 disposals, 2.5 marks, 22.0 hitouts

Van Hattum offers a package that could make him the best player to come out of his draft class. There's little doubt that he makes it as a ruckman; he offers true ruck size with a mature body and the aggression to match an opponent's physicality. What makes him a top five prospect is the traits that other rucks can't provide. Van Hattum is an excellent ball user and routinely gets involved through the midfield, plus has an extraordinary athletic profile that helps him jump all over his opposite number. He offers a glimpse into the future of the ruck position in the AFL.

READ: 'I just hate that' - Harry Van Hattum wants to end ruck disrespect

6. Heath Mellody (6)

Claremont/Western Australia

MID/DEF, 184cm

National Championships: 4 games, 28.2 disposals, 5.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

No prospect ended the season in better form than Mellody. He took out the Larke Medal at the National Championships and ended his season with strong form in the WAFL. Mellody is a natural outside midfielder with an appetite to spread and collect a lot of the ball. He's a lovely kick and bites off damaging options through the corridor and will be a complementary piece across halfback, a wing and eventually on-ball.

READ: WA prospect Heath Mellody is this year's ultimate bolter

7. Gus Teixeira (7)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID, 181cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.0 disposals, 4.2 tackles, 1.8 goals

The power, composure and skill Teixeira plays with gives him a great platform to explode at the next level. He's excellent at navigating through traffic and it gives him a path to becoming an excellent midfielder, but not before he spends time up forward. Teixeira plays with flair and aggression that will hold him in good stead.

8. Mitch Harris (9)

Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

DEF, 195cm

National Championships: 4 games, 8.8 disposals, 3.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Harris is the full package as a key defender. He has the size to play on genuine key forwards, offers athleticism in the air to intercept and good closing speed on the lead. There's upside to his offensive game that excites clubs as well. Harris ended the year with WWT in SANFL finals to rubber stamp his top 10 credentials.

9. Sam Gayfer (8)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

FWD, 194cm

National Championships: 4 games, 11.0 disposals, 4.2 marks, 2.5 goals

Gayfer is the top open pool key forward. A bash-and-crash type with serious courage in the air, he presents at the ball full-chested and flies at everything he can. The combine's new vertical jump record-holder can beat defenders on the lead and in packs, and if his set shot continues to improve Gayfer will be worth every bit of the top 10 price tag.

10. Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) (10)

Giants Academy/Allies

MID, 186cm

National Championships: 2 games, 25.0 disposals, 5.0 marks, 6.0 tackles

Matthews's game is made up of a lot of natural football instinct. He's comfortable operating in stoppages with clean hands and quick decisions, and on the outside has a fluid kicking action off his preferred left that links the chains efficiently. Matthews is a ball magnet because he doesn't fumble and gets to the right spots, and will be the highest picked Giants Academy graduate since Tom Green.

11. Wil Malady (11)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 190cm

National Championships: 3 games, 10.7 disposals, 5.7 marks, 1.3 goals

Malady steps up on the big stage. He was the most dangerous forward in the APS grand final and Talent League grand final to finish the season, and offers a unique blend of traits. He's an excellent runner and can impact off a wing or half forward, but is at his best aerially deep in attack where he launches at the ball with strong hands. Malady hits the scoreboard in a variety of ways which will give him every chance of succeeding in the AFL.

12. Clancy Snell (12)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

DEF, 196cm

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 7.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

Snell's ultra-aggressive intercepting style has seen him come undone at times, but it's also a glimpse into the upside. No one turns defence into attack like the surehanded backman, who loves to roll off his opponent and go third man up, or peel off to intercept and kickstart transition with good foot skills. He needs to hone those defensive instincts as a one-on-one defender which could see him take more time to debut than the other first round key defenders.

13. Leo Steed (13)

Swan Districts/Western Australia

MID, 176cm

National Championships: 4 games, 23.5 disposals, 3.0 marks, 4.0 tackles

Steed is the ultimate professional that gets the absolute best out of himself. He runs hard both ways, wins the ball on the inside and can use it on the outside, and has grown his game outside of the midfield to become a solid contributor ahead of the ball. Steed doesn't let his size impact how damaging he can be as a first-use on-baller..

14. Caylen Murray (Lions Academy) (14)

Lions Academy/Allies

DEF/MID, 183cm

National Championships: 24.0 disposals, 6.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

Murray offers composure and class by the bucket load. He's an assured presence out of the backline that has the foot skills to take kick ins and link play multiple times in passages. There's upside in his composure around stoppages in the future, but he looks a readymade halfback prospect for the Lions.

15. Tyson Bradley (18)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

DEF, 195cm

National Championships: 4 games, 14.5 disposals, 6.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Vic Metro's MVP is all but assured of finding a home in the first round. Bradley plays with an edge and is resolute in not getting beaten. He's strong one-on-one and uses his agility and safe ball use to get himself out of trouble from defence. Bradley's mature body could see him play senior football early next year, and he has leadership ambitions in the future.

16. Jake Eime (15)

Central District/South Australia

DEF, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 20.2 disposals, 3.8 marks, 1.2 tackles

Eime has a point of difference to prospects in the first round with his blazing pace off halfback. He tucks the ball and plays with instinctual dare to break lines and continually put speed on the ball. Eime fits the modern game and will be a weapon off halfback for the club that takes him.

17. Khaled El Souki (Western Bulldogs NGA) (16)

Western Jets/Vic Metro

FWD, 174cm

National Championships: 1 game, 10.0 disposals, 5.0 tackles, 1.0 goals

El Souki is a polarising prospect. Detractors point to his athletic testing and body shape, but you only need to watch the small forward to see how he projects at the next level. El Souki is a balanced power athlete that absorbs hits with a low centre of gravity and plays through contact exceptionally well. He's a lovely kick off his preferred left and routinely hits the scoreboard as a forward-half midfielder, high half forward or deep threat.

READ: 'They'd follow me knowing I kick goals' - NGA-tied Khaled El Souki is in first-round contention

18. Jack Pickett (17)

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

FWD, 194cm

Pickett came into the year as the best key forward in the open pool, but had his season wiped out with an ACL rupture. He's a natural ahead of the ball, timing leads and finding dangerous space before executing set shots with a repeatable action. He has safe hands and looks most at home with the ball out in front of him on the lead.

19. Kodah Edwards (21)

South Adelaide/South Australia

MID, 183cm

National Championships: 4 games, 22.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 3.2 tackles

Edwards rips into every contest like his life depends on it, scrapping for loose balls and thriving in the heat of stoppages. He's also shown flashes of huge upside in the forward 50 where he gets to work as the ball hits the deck and can hit the scoreboard. If Edwards's ball use and decision making comes on at the next level he will prove a steal at this price.

20. Koby LeCras (19)

West Perth/Western Australia

FWD/MID, 192cm

LeCras had his season wiped out due to a partially torn ACL, but not before a best on ground three-goal performance off a wing for the ACL Academy. He can play up the field but is also a target in the forward 50 with the ability to convert opportunities from lead-ups and ground balls. He has real smarts around goals to convert half-chances.

READ: From an ACL tear to a time trial PB - Koby LeCras on building resilience in his draft year

21. Ethan Herbert (20)

North Adelaide/South Australia

RUC/FWD, 200cm

National Championships: 4 games, 15.8 disposals, 3.0 marks, 2.5 tackles

Herbert is the standout ruck in this part of the draft. He has great hands in the contest and wins a lot of his own ball as an extra midfielder, plus has some chops as a forward where he can use his frame and hands to advantage. He should build into being a genuine ruck size and has the all-round game to make it in the AFL.

22. Toby Krasna (24)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

MID, 181cm

National Championships: 3 games, 19.0 disposals, 3.3 marks, 1.0 goals

Krasna plays with freedom and flair as an outside midfielder, taking the ball off the line with a quick few steps and executing his decisions well. He's a slighter frame that gets moved around easily as an inside midfielder so will likely play peripheral positions to begin his career.

23. Noah Williams (22)

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

MID, 177cm

National Championships: 4 games, 15.5 disposals, 4.0 marks, 5.8 tackles

Williams is a hard-nosed inside midfielder that applies himself with courage defensively. He tackles hard and throws his body in harm's way to impact at stoppages. He's also shown the ability to defend well inside his own D50 and offers some run and dash off halfback which is where he likely begins his career.

24. Harvie Cooke (23)

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

MID/FWD, 176cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.5 disposals, 7.0 marks, 1.0 goals

Cooke enjoyed a magnificent season as the Morrish Medallist in the Talent League and an undefeated Vic Metro campaign. He was a strong-bodied midfielder for the Knights then showed some aerial ability as a half forward for Metro. He likely ends up splitting time forward and through the engine room where his smarts can be utilised.

25. George Dimer (31)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

FWD, 173cm

National Championships: 3 games, 16.0 disposals, 5.7 marks, 1.0 goals

Dimer has a lot of tricks to his game. The small forward crumbs packs beautifully and has the burst to get himself out of trouble, but is also super creative to set up teammates in the forward half. He positions himself in dangerous areas consistently, smartly using his body to protect drop zones and create chances for himself and others.

26. Lochie Burrows (29)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro'

181cm, DEF/MID

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 4.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

Burrows is firmly in the mix as a first round pick. He's an ultra-competitive utility, able to provide bounce off halfback, contested gruntwork through the middle or a smaller marking option up forward. His best traits may come as a defensive midfielder with running power and physicality, though he doesn't thrive in any one role.

27. Harrison Chapman (26)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

MID, 190cm

National Championships: 3 games, 18.7 disposals, 4.7 marks, 2.0 tackles

There's serious upside to Chapman with his size, running power and skill. He's a natural outside midfielder and often gets bodied away from the ball in the contest, but in space he can execute and become a metres gained player. He needs to build size to his frame and improve his intensity at times to make it.

28. Marlon Neocleous (25)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD/MID, 168cm

National Championships: 2 games, 16.0 disposals, 5.0 marks, 0.5 goals

Neocleous is a crafty small forward that loves to get amongst the goals and has the celebrations to match. He also doesn't possess the pace to separate from the best lockdown defenders which limits his upside. Neocleous loves to get up the ground and is incisive with his ball use which could be a tool for him to get involved at the next level.

29. Lachie Hicks (35)

Western Jets/Vic Metro

MID, 183cm

National Championships: 16.8 disposals, 4.5 marks, 2.0 tackles

A wildcard pick through the middle rounds. Hicks is an elite athlete that could explode in the right environment. He blends strong endurance with a terrific speed and evasiveness combination that makes him hard to tackle through the contest and a nightmare in open space. Hicks racks up the ball consistently but has issues with his ball use that need to be rounded out.

30. George Gale (33)

Claremont/Western Australia

MID, 190cm

National Championships: 4 games, 27.8 disposals, 5.2 marks, 2.8 tackles

Gale's strong running and mature body should see him play early and often next year. He can play inside and outside of the contest with good discipline and defensive intent, and offered strong contributions for Claremont in his WAFL stints to end the season.

31. Jake Soutar (-)

East Perth

DEF, 190cm

The 20-year-old Soutar may be the best interceptor in the draft crop. He's a natural reader of the play and has sure hands when chopping off attacking forays, plus possesses a big boot and hits the ground running to kickstart transition. Soutar is the best mature-ager available this year.

32. Wil Antrobus (-)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

DEF, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 16.3 disposals, 3.0 marks, 2.8 tackles

There's a clearly defined role for Antrobus at the next level. He's a designated kicker with a sweet left boot, gaining chunks at a time with penetration from deep in defence. The small defender is limited by his size in defensive contests but plays with an edge and offers good run off halfback.

33. Gabe Patterson (27)

Glenelg/South Australia

FWD, 184cm

National Championships: 4 games, 13.0 disposals, 2.5 tackles, 1.0 goals

Patterson plays hard and tough footy in the forward half. He digs in defensively and scraps for loose balls, then grits the teeth and chases with vigour defensively. Offensively he straight lines the ball and plays through contact with power, plus can finish off his chances in front of goal.

34. Jackson Phillips (36)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

182cm, MID

National Championships: 4 games, 16.2 disposals, 3.8 marks, 3.2 tackles

A natural wingman at the next level, Phillips runs hard both ways and uses it safely off his preferred left. He doesn't try to do too much with the ball or take on the risky options, and can fade out of games in those peripheral roles, but projects to have a good floor at the next level with his running and skills.

35. Billy Wigmore (-)

Western Jets/Vic Country

DEF, 189cm

National Championships: 4 games, 17.0 disposals, 5.8 marks, 1.8 tackles

Wigmore is an elite interceptor. He reads the play, peels off and has strong hands in the air. There are worries in how it translates to the next level at his size, but there's no doubting he could have a Tom Stewart-like impact if it all comes together.

36. Keenan Boi (Hawthorn NGA) (28)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

180cm, FWD

National Championships: 3 games, 13.3 disposals, 4.7 marks, 1.0 goals

Boi makes something happen whenever he's around the footy. He's tough and powerful plus applies some of the best defensive pressure you'll see in the draft class. With the ball in hand he makes quick, easy decisions and executes well. There's every chance Boi becomes a reliable pressure forward that can link play up the ground.

37. Albert MacGowan (30)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

187cm, MID

National Championships: 4 games, 22.8 disposals, 6.2 marks, 1.0 tackles

MacGowan finished the year on a tear. He was Sandringham's best player through finals and took out the 2km time trial. There's reason to believe he will become a good winger at the next level; MacGowan is fantastic in the air at his size, runs all day and plays a disciplined role for his side.

38. Sam Devers (previously: 32)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

DEF, 189cm

National Championships: 2 games, 12.0 disposals, 2.5 marks, 1.0 tackles

Devers offers an excellent athletic profile but missed a significant chunk of his top-age year. At his best he can put speed on the ball out of defence, though he's also shown flashes further up the field with his burst. It's likely Devers settles into a lockdown role out of defence where he can use his athleticism to impact.

39. Marcus Prasad (37)

Dandenong Stingrays

167cm, FWD/MID

Talent League: 10 games, 18.6 disposals, 4.8 tackles, 2.0 goals

Prasad has some special traits at his diminutive size. He rarely fumbles below his knees and can draw free kicks with his quickness through contests. He lacks penetration on his preferred left and will struggle to push further up the field at his size, but as a genuine small forward there's a lot to work with.

40. Archie Elliott (-)

GWV Rebels/Vic Country

FWD, 182cm

National Championships: 4 games, 6.0 disposals, 3.5 marks, 1.8 goals

Elliott kept on kicking goals late in the year. He's a good size to impact aerially and when the ball hits the deck, and plays with real confidence around the ball. Elliott can get out the back of his opponent quickly and effectively by reading the contest and has kicked some brilliant goals from open play this year.

41. Blake Justice (Essendon NGA) (-)

Calder Cannons/Vic Metro

MID, 191cm

National Championships: 2 games, 12.0 disposals, 4.5 marks, 0.5 goals

Justice is a unique prospect - he ran fastest across state and national combines for the 20m sprint and his blend of acceleration at his height gives him ample opportunity to win his own ball and explode from contest. Around the ground he gets to a lot of contests and has quick hands but also fades out of games and doesn't have the forward nous required to play multiple roles for a team.

42. Harvey Spawton-Guy (-)

West Perth/Western Australia

FWD/DEF, 196cm

National Championships: 4 games, 8.5 disposals, 4.0 marks, 1.5 goals

Spawton-Guy is a competitor. He fights hard for position in marking contests and invariably brings the ball to ground where he butters up with a physical presence. He's also shown some chops as a resolute key defender and that flexibility appeals to clubs.

43. Mason McGroder (Swans Academy) (-)

Swans Academy/Allies

DEF, 194cm

National Championships: 1 game, 12.0 disposals, 4.0 marks

He's been well-documented since blitzing the national combine, but McGroder is one of the best athletes to enter the AFL system in some time. He turned his back on a pursuit of long jumping after winning silver at the U20 world championships in Oregon this year. He straight lines the ball with blistering pace off halfback and can play way bigger than his frame suggests with an enormous leap. There are significant challenges around his ball skills and reading of the play developing in front of him, but Sydney is a good place for him to develop at the lower levels.

44. Darcy Szerszyn (-)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

DEF, 190cm

National Championships: 4 games, 16.8 disposals, 5.0 marks, 1.0 tackles

Szerszyn is a great size for a defender, able to play on smalls and talls with quickness and physicality. He missed significant chunks of the season through injury but showed a lot of promise coming into his top-age campaign that he could make good on in a professional environment.

45. Jack Slattery (-)

Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

FWD, 191cm

National Championships: 4 games 11.3 disposals, 4.3 marks, 4.0 goals

Slattery was a standout at the National Championships as a rare over-ager. He took advantage of opportunities with an excellent set shot and, while not being a genuine key forward height, used his frame well to protect the ball drop in marking contests and get on the move to find the dangerous space. He should get a shot on an AFL list to continue his rapid development.

46. Xavier Ladbrook (38)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

DEF, 201cm

National Championships: 4 games, 11.5 disposals, 5.5 marks, 0.8 goals

Rated as the fourth key defender in the draft class, Ladbrook is a good runner that has spent time up on a wing or roaming forward as well. He plays within himself with safe ball use and doesn't have the intercepting prowess of Power teammate Snell but offers interesting traits for teams to invest in with the running power at his height. He will need to build size to play down back in the future.

47. Archie Van Dyk (-)

South Adelaide/South Australia

MID, 191cm

National Championships: 1 game, 21.0 disposals, 3.0 marks, 1.0 tackle

Van Dyk excelled against the bigger bodies in the SANFL Reserves and will be at home with the physicality of senior football. He's a tough in-and-under midfielder with great hands under pressure, but limited scope to play outside of the midfield.

48. Benji Van Rooyen (39)

Claremont/Western Australia

203cm, RUC

National Championships: 4 games, 14.0 disposals, 4.0 marks, 20.5 hitouts

Van Rooyen was the best performing ruck at the National Championships. Working against him is the time he may take to develop his conditioning and aerial presence on an AFL list. He's a competitor that, while lacking brother Jacob's athleticism, has safe hands and a selflessness that works alongside his midfielders.

49. Cody Templeton (40)

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 180cm

National Championships: 3 games, 10.3 disposals, 1.3 tackles, 1.7 goals

Templeton saved his best performance for last, booting five goals in the Talent League grand final. The powerful forward can be a difficult matchup; always on the move and able to separate quickly, he's been hot and cold all season and the inconsistency has hurt his stock. His draft range may not begin much earlier than this point but Templeton should get an opportunity on an AFL list.

50. Brady Wright (-)

Werribee VFL

FWD, 195cm

Another mature-ager who produced big numbers in the VFL. Wright is a plug-and-play option up forward with great spatial awareness in marking contests and a reliable set shot routine. He stepped up this year to match the physicality of key defenders and will get his shot on an AFL list.

stories.headline: 'The World Cup never really ended': U.S.-based betting sees rise in wagering on MLS, European soccer
stories.summary: Before the World Cup, many wondered if Americans would stick around afterward. Betting data says yes, they did.
stories.body:
Soccer was the sport of the summer in the United States this year, as the FIFA World Cup came to 11 American cities (in addition to venues in Canada and Mexico). Americans embraced the sport fully, supporting tremendous numbers for television viewership and stadium attendance -- as well as sports betting handle.

BetMGM said that the World Cup "nearly kept pace with the MLB's rigorous summer schedule" despite there being five times as many baseball games over that time period. Hard Rock Bet noted the tournament did three times as much handle and brought in double the number of individual bettors as the men's NCAA tournament, which is traditionally the most-bet-on event on the U.S. sports calendar.

In Colorado, which breaks down betting revenue by sport, the World Cup generated $60.2 million, a near 250% increase from the $17.5 million brought in by the previous edition of the tournament in November 2022.

With European league soccer in full swing and Major League Soccer kicking off playoffs, that momentum has continued over for the American sports betting ecosystem.

BetMGM noted that in the two-month period immediately following the conclusion of the 2026 World Cup, the sportsbook saw a 24.5% year-over-year increase in bets and a 34.5% increase in handle on wagers for club soccer. Hard Rock said there have been nearly 30% more wagers on soccer overall, specifically 43% more in the Premier League and 21% in the Champions League with World Cup stars Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland and Harry Kane attracting double the amount of bets in the competition compared to the same time period last year.

"The World Cup never really ended for our customers. The bettors who did well backing Mbappé, Haaland and Kane this summer have followed them straight back to the Champions League, and the post-World Cup pain continues for us every time those guys light up the scoreboard," Hard Rock Bet SVP of sportsbook Neil Walsh told ESPN over email. "Those Tuesday and Wednesday afternoon matches don't compete with primetime U.S. sports, so they get our customers' full attention."

"We have seen an immediate increase in activity across our soccer markets when comparing 2026 with 2025," Caesars lead soccer trader Mark Bickerdike said in an email.

"Encouragingly, that growth is evident across both pre-match and in-play betting and is reflected across the majority of competitions we offer. It certainly feels as though we've benefited from the momentum generated by the World Cup heading into the new domestic seasons."

MLS has attracted significantly more betting action in 2026 than it did the year before, showing a 30.4% increase in tickets and a 38.8% increase in money from mid-July to the end of October. MLS handle is up 27% at Hard Rock Bet over a similar time period, with Inter Miami -- a fixture for the Florida-based book -- garnering almost 40% more bets year-over-year.

"We've seen a jump up in more users that are betting soccer and a lot of that is from MLS," DraftKings director of sports operations Johnny Avello told ESPN. "We'd like to think that's from people betting the World Cup this year and finding out that soccer's a fun game to wager on."

The development of MLS' betting market comes in the wake of unprecedented popularity for the league and as it looks to transition to a fall-spring schedule that lines up with the rest of world soccer.

Bickerdike said that since Aug. 1, MLS has moved from being Caesars' fourth-most bet soccer league to second. The revised calendar could benefit the league further.

"It creates the opportunity for customers to engage with a full day of soccer, starting with competitions such as the Premier League and LaLiga before moving into a slate of MLS fixtures later in the day," said Bickerdike. "From a sportsbook perspective, our market offering is consistent across these competitions, creating a seamless experience for customers and potentially encouraging greater engagement with MLS over time."

Coming out of MLS Decision Day on Saturday, Nashville SC are the favorites for the MLS Cup at +400. Thomas Müller's Vancouver Whitecaps and Lionel Messi's Inter Miami (the reigning champions) follow just behind at +450.
